Epiphyseal Plate (Physeal) Fractures
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Pediatric bone is more elastic, leading to unique fracture patterns, including torus (buckle)
fractures and greenstick fractures.
The thicker periosteum generally remains intact on the side of the bone toward which the
distal fragment is displaced.
This periosteal hinge facilitates reduction.
Aggressive reduction attempts may disrupt the hinge, making satisfactory reduction more
difficult.
Open physes (epiphyseal plates) can allow for remodeling and straightening of a malunited
fracture; however, with growth disturbance, ongoing growth may result in angular deformity,
limb-length discrepancy, or both.
Remodeling occurs more rapidly and predictably in the plane of joint motion (eg, sagittal
malalignment at the wrist remodels more successfully than coronal plane deformity).
In the upper extremity, the fastest growth occurs at the upper and lower ends of the
extremity (ie, at the proximal humerus and distal radius and ulna), whereas in the lower
extremity, most growth occurs in the middle (ie, at the distal femur and proximal tibia and
fibula). Fracture remodeling is best for fractures close to physes, especially those physes with
the most growth potential.
Fractures most commonly occur through the hypertrophic zone.

Overview
The pediatric skeleton is less mineralized and more porous, resulting in a lower modulus
of elasticity. This unique property allows for more absorption of energy before fracture,
leading to unique fracture patterns in children. Two incomplete fracture patterns that
are commonly seen in the care of injured children are torus (or buckle) fractures and
greenstick fractures. Torus fractures are a consequence of an axial load and result in
failure on the compression side or concavity. Greenstick fractures are a consequence of
bending stresses and result in failure on the tension or convex side. Plastic deformation
also can occur and is most commonly located in the diaphysis. This is identified as

angular or rotational deformity resulting from internal microscopic failure of the bone
without the presence of an obvious fracture.
Children also have a thick periosteum covering the bone that often is intact on the
concavity of the fracture or on the side in which the bone displaces. This produces a
periosteal hinge that is useful in obtaining and maintaining a reduction. This hinge can
be disrupted with the original injury or with aggressive attempts at reduction.
Satisfactory reduction may be much more challenging to achieve if a periosteal hinge is
not present.
Another unique aspect of pediatric bones is the presence of a physis (growth plate or
epiphyseal plate). This structure is responsible for the main source of remodeling or
straightening of a malunited fracture. Remodeling occurs most efficiently in deformities
that are present along the plane of joint motion. The correction also is greatest if
considerable growth potential is present. This includes younger children and growth
plates with the most growth potential. In the upper extremity, the proximal humerus
and the distal radius provide most of the growth and, therefore, possess the greatest
remodeling potential. This is true for the distal femur and the proximal tibia in the lower
extremity. Remodeling potential has limits based on the degree of malunion and a child’s
overall growth remaining.
Approximately 25% of fractures in children involve the physis.1 Physeal fractures are
thought to occur most commonly through the zone of provisional calcification in the
hypertrophic zone.2 Therefore, the cleavage plane of Salter-Harris type I and type II
fractures occurs through the hypertrophic zone and leaves the germinal layer of the
physis intact and attached to the epiphysis. This allows normal growth to resume after
most physeal Salter-Harris type I and type II fractures. Salter-Harris type III and type IV
injuries disrupt the germinal layer, leading to an increased risk of physeal arrest. In
addition, physes with an undulating contour, such as the distal femur and distal tibia,
have been found to experience physeal fractures that propagate through multiple layers
of the physis,3 predisposing these areas to a higher risk of physeal arrest. Most physeal
fractures heal rapidly and possess considerable potential for remodeling. These same
fractures also can result in growth disturbance and persistent or subsequent deformity.

Injury Classification
The most used classification is the Salter-Harris classification system4 (Figure 1).
Advantages: ease of use and prognostic value
Disadvantage: Salter-Harris type V axial crush fractures, which are rare, cannot be
distinguished from Salter-Harris type I fractures on initial presentation; the differentiation
cannot be made until growth arrest has occurred.
Figure 1 Illustration shows the Salter-Harris classification of fractures. Type I is characterized by
physeal separation. Type II is characterized by a fracture line that extends transversely through
the physis and exits through the metaphysis. Type III is characterized by a fracture that traverses
the physis and exits through the epiphysis. Type IV is characterized by a fracture line that passes
through the epiphysis, across the physis, and out the metaphysis. Type V is a crush injury to the
physis. (Reproduced from Kay RM, Matthys GA: Pediatric ankle fractures: Evaluation and
treatment. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2001;9[4]:268-278.)

Injury Classification
The Salter-Harris classification is the most commonly used classification system for
physeal fractures. This classification system is easy to use and facilitates communication
between providers. The classification system also provides prognosis with regard to the
risk of physeal disturbance, with Salter-Harris type I and type II fractures being

IV fractures. A Salter-Harris type V fracture is commonly diagnosed months after an
injury when a growth arrest becomes apparent.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Growth arrest after physeal fracture
Recognition—After fracture healing, Park-Harris lines should be moving away from the physis
while remaining parallel to the physis. If the lines are not moving away from or are not
parallel to the physis, then growth arrest (partial or whole) has occurred (Figure 2).

distal tibia fracture complicated by medial growth arrest demonstrates a 1.7-cm leg-length
disparity and a 15° varus deformity of the ankle. Growth-disturbance lines (arrow) converge
medially because of the medial growth arrest. (Reproduced from Kay RM, Matthys GA: Pediatric
ankle fractures: evaluation and treatment. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2001;9[4]:268-278.)

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Physeal fractures require adequate follow-up to identify growth disturbances secondary
to a traumatic injury to the physis. A concern for a physeal injury is present if a Park-
Harris line tapers towards the physis in an oblique manner (Figure 3, A). Radiographs
should demonstrate Park-Harris lines that are parallel to the physis while progressing
away from the physis with growth (Figure 3, B). The presence of sclerosis and loss of the
radiolucency between the epiphysis and metaphysis with alteration in normal physeal
contour also increases concern for a physeal injury. Physeal growth disturbances are
observed in approximately 10% of patients with a physeal fracture, with rates varying
greatly between specific anatomic locations.5 Physeal fractures of the distal femur,
proximal tibia, and distal tibia are associated with the highest rates of physeal
disturbance.6 An increased likelihood of physeal arrest has been associated with the
number of reduction attempts. This is the one variable that is modifiable by the treating
physician.7 All physeal fractures should be manipulated gently and only under adequate
sedation to minimize iatrogenic trauma to the physis.

Imaging Studies
Advanced imaging studies, particularly MRI, facilitate determination of physeal bar size and
location. Currently, CT can be used but is associated with radiation exposure.

Imaging Studies
If a physeal disturbance is suspected in a patient with considerable growth remaining,
advanced imaging studies often are used to identify the physeal injury and define its size
and location. CT and MRI have been used for this purpose, but only MRI avoids radiation
exposure to the patient. Both imaging modalities can be used to map out the physis to

Management
Based on physeal bar size and location and the amount of growth remaining in the affected
bone
Upper extremity growth arrest results in fewer functional problems than lower extremity
growth arrest and less commonly requires management; however, growth arrest in the distal
radius or the ulna may lead to a profound change in ulnar variance that may necessitate
surgical management.
Sequelae from lower extremity physeal disturbances typically manifest as limb-length
inequality, angular deformity, and/or joint malformation. Similar to the wrist, injury of the
growth of one bone may lead to symptomatic overgrowth of the neighboring bone, with
fibular impingement occurring after a distal tibia growth arrest.
Physeal bar excision: Attempts at excision (with interposition of an inert material, such as
autogenous fat or methyl methacrylate) may be considered for bars less than 33% to 50% of
the cross-sectional area of the physis and in a physis with more than 2 years of remaining
growth. Results of physeal bar excision are best with small bars in younger children.

Management
Physeal arrest may lead to limb-length inequalities and/or limb deformities. These
typically are less bothersome in the upper extremities and, therefore, less commonly
require surgical management. The most common sequela of lower extremity physeal
disturbance is deformity about the knee after a distal femur or proximal tibial physeal
injury.
Because these are rapidly growing physes, abnormalities should be identified promptly
and management should be initiated because considerable genu varum/valgum or limb-
length inequality may occur quickly. Management of a physeal disturbance is based on
the size of the bar and the amount of growth remaining of the physis. If more than 2
years of growth is remaining and the physeal bar is less than 50% of the cross-sectional

by excising or removing the bony bridge and placing an inert material, such as
autogenous fat or methyl methacrylate, as a spacer in the area of the excision.
Outcomes are best in young patients with small, central bars. Prognosis is best with less
time from injury to excision.6 If the physeal bar is large (>50%) or the patient has less
than 2 years of growth remaining, then epiphysiodesis should be considered. If
substantial growth remains yet physeal bar excision is not indicated, epiphysiodesis
should be considered. Epiphysiodesis can be performed with the use of drills and
curettes to ablate the physis or with the use of transphyseal screws. Partial arrest
requires epiphysiodesis of the portion of the physis that is continuing to grow to prevent
additional deformity. If limb-length inequality is predicted to be 2 to 5 cm, contralateral
epiphysiodesis is indicated. If the discrepancy is projected to be greater than 5 cm, limb
lengthening should be considered.
Surgical Management
Indications
Existing or developing angular or length deformities in patients with substantial growth
remaining
Management should be considered if limb-length inequality is anticipated to be greater than
2 cm.8
Concomitant osteotomy should be considered if deformity is greater than 15° to 20°.9
Arrest of the bones of the forearm or leg may lead to overgrowth of the neighboring bone (ie,
ulnar overgrowth in patients with physeal arrest distal radius).
Surgical treatment typically is recommended in patients with physeal arrest of the distal
radius if more than 2 mm of ulnar growth remains.10
Additional shortening of the ulna may be required if pain secondary to ulnocarpal abutment
is present.10
Contraindications
Minimal growth or no growth remaining and asymptomatic

Bony bridge is excised followed by placement of an inert material, such as autogenous fat or
cranioplast, as a spacer in the area of the excision.
Outcomes
Outcomes are best in young patients with small, central bars. Prognosis is best with less time
from injury to excision.6
Epiphysiodesis
Indications
Patient with less than 2 years of growth remaining or a physeal bar greater than 50% of the
cross-sectional area of the physis
Ipsilateral extremity: If angular deformity is developing, the functioning part of the affected
physis may be ablated to prevent increasing deformity.
Contralateral epiphysiodesis is considered if the physeal arrest will result in unacceptable
limb-length discrepancy, typically 2 cm or larger, in the lower extremities.
Contraindications
Minimal growth remaining with mild deformity present
Techniques/Procedures
Percutaneous epiphysiodesis with ablation
Percutaneous epiphysiodesis with the use of transphyseal screws

Pediatric Polytrauma and Upper Extremity Fractures
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Polytrauma is the occurrence of a life-threatening or limb-threatening injury, an injury to more
than one organ system, or multiple long bone fractures.11
As many as 63% of pediatric polytrauma patients sustain musculoskeletal injuries.12
Appropriate treatment of polytrauma patients requires a multidisciplinary team.

Overview

Patients who experience severe trauma have a high likelihood of multiple injuries;
therefore, appropriate management may be complex. A team approach involving
pediatric trauma surgeons, pediatricians, and other pediatric surgical subspecialties if
indicated, often is required. Because most polytrauma patients sustain musculoskeletal
injuries, orthopaedic surgeons must be knowledgeable on the treatment of pediatric
polytrauma patients.
Epidemiology
Trauma is the most common cause of death in children older than 1 year.
The most common causes are falls and motor vehicle collisions.
Many injuries and deaths can be avoided by appropriate use of child seats and restraints.
Cervical spine injuries after a motor vehicle collision are more common in children younger
than 8 years. Two contributing elements are restraints that do not fit young children well and
the disproportionately large size of the head relative to the trunk. Deceleration mechanisms
lead to distraction injuries.
Orthopaedic injuries are the second most common cause of morbidity.
Pediatric polytrauma patients treated at a pediatric trauma center experience 20% lower
mortality rates.13

Epidemiology
Trauma is the leading cause of death in individuals aged 1 to 19 years.14 Most
polytrauma injuries result from a fall from a height or motor vehicle collision and are
considered preventable. Appropriate use of child safety restraints may decrease the
number of injuries in children. Anatomic differences in young children may predispose
pediatric patients to certain injuries. Children younger than 8 years more commonly
sustain upper cervical spine injuries. This is thought to be because of the
disproportionate head size in children and poor fit of safety restraints.15 The most
common cause of morbidity after polytrauma is head injury, followed by musculoskeletal

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Initial Evaluation, Resuscitation, and Transport
Hypotension (systolic blood pressure =98 mm Hg) and low Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score on
initial evaluation are strongly associated with increased risk of in-hospital mortality after
trauma.
Fluid resuscitation
If venous access is difficult, intraosseous infu­sion with a large-bore needle may be necessary.
Dissimilar from adults, children often remain hemody­namically stable for extended periods
after substantial blood loss. Hypovolemic shock eventually ensues if fluid resuscitation is
inadequate.
Blood volume: 70 mL/kg
Hypotension develops in children with loss of 25% of blood volume.
Because young children have a large head size, a special transport board with an occipital
cutout or a mattress pad to elevate the body is necessary in transporting children younger
than 6 years to the hospital; this is done to prevent cervical spine flexion and potential
iatrogenic cervical spinal cord injury.

Initial Evaluation, Resuscitation, and Transport
The initial evaluation and resuscitation of a polytrauma patient follows Advanced
Trauma Life Support protocol and Pediatric Advanced Life Support protocol, which can
be remembered as the ABCDEs (airway, breathing, circulation, disability, exposure). This
begins with assessment and stabilization of the ABCs to address any life-threatening
issues. The next step includes a quick disability or neurologic assessment, which includes
a GCS score. The final portion of the primary survey includes exposure, in which the
clothing is removed for a rapid examination, and the patient is then recovered to
prevent hypothermia. Findings gathered during these initial steps may provide
information regarding the likelihood of future in-hospital mortality because an increase

is observed in patients with systolic blood pressure lower than 98 mm Hg and a GCS
score of 3 on presentation.16
Each system under the ABCs must be stabilized before the process can move forward.
Hypotension is addressed in the circulation assessment. Two large-bore intravenous
catheters are placed for resuscitation. Occasionally, this is not possible in pediatric
patients secondary to the small size of accessible veins. In these patients, intraosseous
catheters can be used for rapid fluid replacement by placing a large-bore needle in the
proximal tibia just distal to the tuberosity. A urinary catheter to monitor urine output
also may aid in assessing adequacy of organ perfusion, and a central venous catheter
may be used in patients with severe trauma. Overhydration may lead to cerebral edema,
causing elevated intracranial pressures and exacerbating traumatic brain injury.
Similar to adults, appropriate fluid resuscitation is critical to maintain organ perfusion.
Dissimilar from adults, the strong cardiovascular system of pediatric patients can
maintain an adequate hemodynamic status for an extended period despite considerable
blood loss. Early signs of hypovolemia may be tachycardia, and this must be considered
so early volume replacement can occur before hypotension. The primary goal of
appropriate resuscitation is to prevent acidosis, hypothermia, and coagulopathy, also
known as the lethal triad.14 Children can maintain adequate blood pressures with blood
volume losses of as much as 25%. Because blood volumes vary greatly in children based
on size and age, a quick calculation can be used for estimation by considering 70 mL of
blood per kilogram of weight of the child.
Another unique consideration for pediatric trauma patients pertains to the cervical
spine. The relatively larger head size compared to trunk size of children creates a
position of flexion of the cervical spine if the child is positioned flat on a standard trauma
board. To appropriately immobilize the cervical spine in a neutral position, a pediatric
trauma board with an occipital recess is used or the body of the child is elevated on a
small mattress (Figure 4).

Systemic Response to Trauma
Timing of multiorgan failure in children differs from that in adults, occurring almost
immediately after injury and simultaneously rather than in a stepwise fashion.
Rate of acute lung injury in children is one-sixth as frequent as that in adults.
Children mount a strong local inflammatory response to facilitate healing compared with
adults (Table 1).

Systemic Response to Trauma
The physiologic response to polytrauma has been found to differ between pediatric and
adult patients. This is thought to lead to a much lower rate of multisystem organ failure
in pediatric polytrauma patients. Multisystem organ failure has been noted to occur in
approximately 3% of children, compared with rates as high as 40% in adults who sustain
severe trauma.17,18 If multisystem organ failure occurs in pediatric patients, it typically is
observed early in the course of treatment, during the resuscitation phase, and is
associated with simultaneous involvement of all organ systems.17,19 This is in contrast to
adults, who typically experience organ failure beginning 48 hours after admission and
have a sequential onset beginning with the pulmonary system.17,19-21 This coincides
with a likelihood of acute lung injury one-sixth as frequent in children compared with
adults.22,23 These differences in response to trauma lead to an overall increased
inflammatory response locally at a tissue level and a decreased systemic inflammatory
response in pediatric patients. This, in turn, leads to an enhanced ability for tissue repair
at the local level while generating less systemic harm24 (Resource 1).

Secondary Evaluation
After the primary survey has been performed and the ABCDEs addressed, the patient
should then, and only then, undergo a secondary evaluation. This is the time at which
the patient's history is obtained and a comprehensive physical examination is
performed. The provider should progress through the evaluation in a structured manner
to include the head, neck, spine, thorax, abdomen, and extremities.
Head injuries are a common cause of mortality and morbidity and, therefore, need to be
identified and managed promptly. A GCS score of less than 8 should initiate a
neurosurgical evaluation because this has been determined to be a level associated with
a higher risk of mortality. The GCS score at 72 hours after admission may provide
prognostic information regarding potential morbidity.25
Pediatric patients can sustain injury to multiple organ systems in the setting of trauma.
Because of the small size of the patient, multiple organs are located in close proximity,
providing opportunity for simultaneous organ injury. The surface of the chest, abdomen,
and pelvis are inspected for signs of injury. The classic scenario is the presence of a lap
belt sign, or abdominal bruising secondary to injury from the seatbelt. This bruising

pattern should increase concern for an intra-abdominal injury and a concomitant lumbar
spine injury, most commonly a Chance fracture or flexion-distraction injury.
Another unique characteristic of pediatric anatomy is the pliable nature of the immature
skeleton. This allows the energy encountered to be transferred to the internal organs
while avoiding an obvious fracture of the surrounding bony structures.26
The secondary evaluation requires a systematic approach so injuries are not missed.
Reports identify that as many as 10% of injuries are missed initially secondary to the
presence of a head injury or a distracting injury (Resources 2 and 3). After this portion
has been completed, definitive stabilization of injuries is performed.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
The standard trauma radiographic series obtained during the primary survey consists of an AP
radiograph of the chest, AP radiograph of the pelvis, and a lateral radiograph of the cervical
spine.
Orthogonal images of extremity injuries should be obtained after the patient is stable.

Radiography
A recent study demonstrated a low rate of patients (6.6%) in whom injuries were
identified on trauma series radiographs if the GCS score was greater than 12 and the
physical examination did not suggest an injury. This has led to questioning of the utility
of full trauma series radiographs in an alert and cooperative child with a normal physical
examination.26
Areas of suspected injuries to the extremities are identified during the secondary survey.
After the patient is hemodynamically stable, orthogonal radiographs should be obtained.

Overview
Open fractures occur if a soft-tissue injury in the vicinity of a fracture allows access for
contamination of the fracture site. Bacterial infection may result, which may lead to
persistent infection, nonunion, bone loss, and the need for additional procedures. Most

resulting in high rates of amputation, infection, and growth disturbance.

injury and the amount of surgical management required, psychological sequelae may
occur. This should be considered in patients who sustain severe trauma and require
extensive treatment.
Outcomes
Pediatric open fractures are associated with better outcomes and lower infection rates
compared with adult open fractures.
Successful outcomes should be expected in most pediatric patients with an open fracture if
treatment is performed appropriately.
